changes.after: A future represents work that can be driven later. Making it does not run the body of this async block.

before: An async block produces a Future value describing work. Its body progresses only when the future is polled. Creating the future does not spawn a thread, start a timer or install an executor. This example deliberately drops an unpolled future.

The .await syntax is allowed inside an async function or block, not this ordinary main. An executor is responsible for polling and wakeups for general asynchronous work. No Tokio or other runtime is used here; the next lesson polls only an already-ready standard-library future once, not arbitrary I/O.
Expected output or behavior: created. Compiler evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.

Optional local transfer task: Explain why writing async alone provides neither a thread nor a general I/O runtime. You may trace it without a Rust compiler; reading completion is not proof of a local run.

before.question: If drop(future) is replaced by future.await in this ordinary main, what happens?
choices: The body has already run before created was printed.
The compiler installs a general-purpose executor.
Compilation rejects await outside an async context.
before.explanation: A future remains lazy, and .await has a language context requirement; a normal main cannot use it directly.

after.question: Could this ordinary main function use `.await` directly?
choices: Yes. Dropping a future makes it run.
No. Await needs an async context.
after.explanation: This main function is not async, so Rust rejects await here.
